cells.name: Continuity and responsiveness
cells.example: T3 answers T1 and T2 directly; T8 takes up T7's distrust of the word bet.
cells.limitation: T10 opens a new financial-relief thread without engaging T9's comparison point.

cells.name: Development of ideas
cells.example: T7 introduces reversibility, absent from openings; T8 and section E build on it.
cells.limitation: T11 mostly recaps the three worries and adds no new distinction.

cells.name: Exploration of central tensions
cells.example: T5 reframes time cost as what the displaced hours were going to hold.
cells.limitation: Career upside raised in T6 and T8 is never weighed against the hours.

cells.name: Integration of perspectives
cells.example: T4 narrows Kahneman's claim after T3; T11 agrees on method, not verdict.
cells.limitation: T10's point that a raise can buy relief is taken up by no other mind.

cells.name: Progress toward understanding
cells.example: Section D reframes the question around displaced hours, felt commute and reversibility.
cells.limitation: T11 closes on a recap rather than sharpening the disputed weight of discomfort.

cells.name: Faithful engagement
cells.example: T3 turns Kahneman's own misprediction point against T2 accurately.
cells.limitation: T5 sets aside T3's usable-train-time point with only 'eats the same hours'.

cells.name: Substance of challenges
cells.example: T7 names the assumption that a bet is costless to exit; T8 answers with reversibility.
cells.limitation: T1's assumption that all three hours are new time goes unchallenged.

cells.name: Accuracy and support
cells.example: T1's arithmetic holds: three hours a day over five days is fifteen hours.
cells.limitation: T2 and T4 attribute commute findings to Kahneman's book (suspected stretch); T4 generalisation unsupported.

cells.name: Calibration and transparency
cells.example: T10 marks its view as 'mine and not Thoreau'; T2 marks 'I would go further'.
cells.limitation: T4 states commuters 'usually' stare instead of reading as fact without support.

cells.name: Intellectual honesty and revision
cells.example: T4 'Fair, and it narrows my claim'; T7 concedes the trial ride.
cells.limitation: T10 softens the Auditor's T1 stance naming no earlier argument as cause.

cells.name: Identification of the actual concern
cells.example: Section A and T6 treat 'how do I decide' as a method question, not a verdict.
cells.limitation: Whether the user already leans one way is never asked.

cells.name: Meaningful use of personal context
cells.example: T1 converts the 90-minute figure into fifteen weekly hours.
cells.limitation: T1 leaves the 25% versus hours comparison as a guess instead of using both figures.

cells.name: Fit with goals and values
cells.example: Section D keeps the minds' leanings separate from the user's ideal-Tuesday question.
cells.limitation: The user's own priorities are asked only once, in section D, not in the debate.

cells.name: Attention to constraints and stakes
cells.example: T5 names sleep, bedtime and exercise as hypothetical displaced hours.
cells.limitation: Money costs of commuting appear only in sections A and E, never in the debate.

cells.name: Responsiveness to information
cells.example: T3 asks the commute mode; T8 branches on reversibility.
cells.limitation: Current commute length never asked; T1 counts all three hours as new cost.

cells.name: Clarification of desires and motivations
cells.example: T10 offers relief from debt or insecurity as one possible reason for the raise.
cells.limitation: Motives (relief, career, escaping current job) never set side by side with a question.

cells.name: Examination of assumptions
cells.example: T9 exposes the vividly imagined new job against a barely imagined old one.
cells.limitation: The assumption that the raise itself is the main gain is examined only late, T10.

cells.name: Clarification of values and priorities
cells.example: Section D's ideal-Tuesday question sets time against what the income would do.
cells.limitation: No turn asks the user to rank time, money and career directly.

cells.name: Recognition of fears and outside expectations
cells.example: T10 names debt and insecurity; T7 names family and lease ties.
cells.limitation: Outside expectations, such as the status of a raise, are not examined.

cells.name: Agency and reflective ownership
cells.example: T9 invites listing current-job dislikes; T10 asks the price be named aloud.
cells.limitation: T10's naming-the-price invitation is not turned into a question the user answers.

cells.name: Definition of the decision and options
cells.example: T6 adds learning first; section E adds declining or negotiating.
cells.limitation: Negotiation appears only in section E and is never discussed in the debate.

cells.name: Explanation of tradeoffs
cells.example: T8 weighs a capped downside against locking in a move or mortgage.
cells.limitation: Fares or fuel costs of the commute are never weighed against the raise.

cells.name: Identification of decisive conditions
cells.example: Section E: seated reliable route and remote days favour accepting; stop-and-go favours declining.
cells.limitation: T1 leaves per-hour value of the raise as 'I suspect'; 'within a year' is ungrounded.

cells.name: Treatment of uncertainty
cells.example: Section E's last branch lists the unknowns to learn before deciding.
cells.limitation: Unknowns are listed but not ranked by which would change the choice most.

cells.name: Proportionate next steps
cells.example: T6: ride the route at real rush hour and ask about remote days.
cells.limitation: T6's 'twice' is not derived from anything the user said.

cells.name: Accessible language
cells.example: T1 'a second part-time job that pays nothing' states the cost plainly.
cells.limitation: The label Hedonic Accountant in section B is unexplained jargon.

cells.name: Traceable arguments and references
cells.example: T3 'Kahneman, your own point' and T8 'That is exactly the variable' point clearly.
cells.limitation: T9 'the comparison' maps to no single turn; minds called by author, not title.

cells.name: Manageable pacing and turn length
cells.example: Eleven turns, all within the word range, each making one move.
cells.limitation: Turn lengths are near-uniform across the debate, flattening pace somewhat.

cells.name: Distinguishable positions and voices
cells.example: T11 states three distinct worries: wear, displacement, missing facts.
cells.limitation: T10 steps outside the Auditor's voice with 'mine and not Thoreau'.

cells.name: Economy and sustained attention
cells.example: Most turns add one new consideration without recap.
cells.limitation: T11 recaps the three worries that section D then restates again.

cells.name: Meaningful stakes and tension
cells.example: T5 'If they were the best part of the day, no raise repays them.'
cells.limitation: Tension stays polite throughout; no exchange becomes a sharp clash.

cells.name: Surprise and reversals
cells.example: T4 narrows its claim, citing T3's train-versus-highway point as the cause.
cells.limitation: T10's softening of the Auditor names no earlier argument as cause.

cells.name: Personality and expressive voice
cells.example: T7 'wiser than philosophizing from a chair' gives the Auditor a dry wit.
cells.limitation: T10 breaks the Auditor's persona; Kahneman's voice stays analytic and plain.

cells.name: Memorable delivery
cells.example: T4 'people usually forecast they will read, and then... stare at the window.'
cells.limitation: Few analogies beyond T1's part-time job; most turns are plain exposition.

cells.name: Anticipation and emotional movement
cells.example: T5's bedtime image shifts the debate from arithmetic to lived hours.
cells.limitation: T11 ends on a summary, leaving the close emotionally flat.

strengths: T7 to T8: the Auditor's objection to the word bet yields reversibility, which shapes section E.
T3 to T4: the Hedonic Accountant narrows its claim and names T3's commute-type point as the cause.
Section E gives observable conditions (seated route, remote days, displaced sleep) with the option each favours.
weaknesses: T1 counts all three daily hours as new cost; the user's current commute is never asked.
T1 leaves the per-hour value of the 25% raise as a guess though the user's figures allow the comparison.
T10: the Life-Cost Auditor softens its stance with no cause named, and no mind answers the relief point.

symptoms.observed: Treats all fifteen weekly hours as new cost; current commute length never asked.
symptoms.evidence: Three hours a day is fifteen hours a week

symptoms.observed: Per-hour value of the raise left as a guess, not compared from the user's figures.
Auditor softens its T1 stance and names no earlier argument as cause.
symptoms.evidence: I will add something that is mine and not Thoreau

symptoms.observed: Generalisation about commuters stated as fact with no support.
symptoms.evidence: people usually forecast they will read, and then they just stare

symptoms.observed: Closing turn recaps three worries that section D restates again.
symptoms.evidence: Kahneman worries the commute will wear on you, Thoreau worries

findings.description: Commute non-adaptation and stop-and-go effects come mainly from commuting research, not clearly from Thinking, Fast and Slow; the attribution may stretch the book.
Claim that commuters usually forecast reading and then stare out the window is stated as fact with no support.
Persona bases name real books; the worker could not browse and no source evidence is attached.

rubric_fit_notes: The user gave only two facts, so C3.2 and C3.3 have little personal context to use; ratings judge use of what was given. T1 arithmetic checked: 3 hours x 5 days = 15 hours.
question_type_note: Read as a decision question; every cell applied as written, with options including learning first and negotiating.
